analysis.one_liner: Eliminates qualified immunity, letting victims sue government officials for constitutional violations.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors in the final weeks of the 116th Congress, never received a hearing or a vote and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Qualified immunity is a judge-made rule that shields government workers — most often police officers — from being personally sued for violating someone's constitutional rights, unless the victim can point to an earlier court case that clearly established those rights in that exact situation. This bill would amend the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to wipe out that defense entirely, so an officer or official could not escape a lawsuit by claiming they acted in good faith or that the right was not clearly established at the time. It was introduced on December 16, 2020, with no cosponsors, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose constitutional rights are violated by government employees — police misconduct victims especially — would gain the ability to hold individual officers personally liable in court, instead of seeing cases dismissed under qualified immunity. Cities would not face new direct costs under the bill's text, but lawsuits against individual officers would become easier to bring and harder to dismiss early.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of government and police misconduct

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends 42 U.S.C. 1983 so that good faith, a reasonable belief that conduct was lawful, and the absence of a clearly established right can no longer be used as defenses in civil rights lawsuits against government actors.

Qualified immunity is a judicially created doctrine that protects government employees or people acting with state authority from personal liability for constitutional violations; eliminating it would make it easier for victims to reach a jury and recover damages.

analysis.who_pays: Government employees — above all law enforcement officers — who would lose personal protection from damages lawsuits, along with the municipalities, unions, and insurers who typically pay or defend against those judgments. Government lawyers would face more litigation that currently gets dismissed at an early stage.

drawbacks.text: The bill offered no transition period or limits: it would expose individual officers to personal liability even when they acted reasonably under the law as they understood it, a change that opponents of qualified-immunity reform argue could make it harder to recruit and retain police and drive up liability insurance costs for local governments.

The bill was a one-page measure introduced with zero cosponsors and no committee action, so it never received scrutiny, amendments, or a public hearing that could have tested or refined these trade-offs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people harmed by constitutional violations, the gain is real: qualified immunity is the single most common reason civil rights lawsuits against officers are thrown out before trial. The cost falls on individual officers and the governments that back them, in the form of personal damages exposure and higher defense costs. An honest assessment is that the bill's goal was significant but its design was bare-bones — no hearing, no debate, no compromise language such as capping individual liability while shifting payouts to employers — and it was introduced so late in a dying Congress that it had no realistic path forward.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Kwanza Hall introduced the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act on December 16, 2020, with no cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill would have eliminated the defenses of good faith and 'not clearly established' law in civil actions under 42 U.S.C. 1983 for deprivation of constitutional rights.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government employees and the police departments, unions, and municipalities that back them are better off: because the bill never advanced, qualified immunity remains available as a defense, and civil rights suits against individual officers can still be dismissed on that basis. Officers and their insurers avoided the personal damages exposure the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Kwanza Hall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act and delivered introductory remarks on December 16, 2020.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: House members generally
against.role: None of the 430 other Representatives cosponsored the bill
against.what_they_did: No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no party ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: Officers are the most frequent defendants in 42 U.S.C. 1983 lawsuits, and qualified immunity is the doctrine most often used to end those suits before trial; abolishing it would remove that shield. The industry's interest in keeping the doctrine runs directly against the public's ability to hold officers personally accountable.

industries.industry: Municipal governments and their liability insurers
industries.note: Ending qualified immunity would mean more suits reaching settlement or judgment and higher defense and insurance costs for local governments. Governments would also face stronger incentives to supervise and train officers, which is where the public benefit lies.
